entries.test: Microsoft's quarterly financial disclosures and public evidence of generative AI revenue, costs, and customer returns would establish the spending, spending plans, and financial benefits.
entries.note: The quarter is the one ending June 30, 2024; 'much money' is relative to the investment discussed.
'Probably' qualifies the explanation, including both high expenses and lack of returns.

entries.test: Public deal terms, staffing records, and evidence of Character.ai's continuing independent development and operations would test whether Google effectively acquired its business and left it nonviable.
entries.note: 'Effectively dead' has an operational reading in the surrounding discussion of lost staff and model exclusivity.
The preceding sentence supplies the broader unsustainability inference; the financial explanation is expressly qualified by 'likely'.

entries.test: Public financing, acquisition, and infrastructure commitments would show whether AI financial exposure was increasingly concentrated in the named technology companies.
entries.note: The following sentence supplies the named companies and the comparison with startups and investors.

entries.test: Public investment agreements, cloud-credit disclosures, and infrastructure spending reports would establish OpenAI's and Anthropic's dependence on billions in subsidized cloud compute.
entries.note: The welfare metaphor accompanies a concrete financing claim.
This asserts a possibility, not a minimum delay.
The concrete consequence for OpenAI's plans is qualified by 'might'.

entries.test: Contemporaneous customer interviews, investor statements, and reporting on OpenAI's product and financing position would test the stated customer expectations and need for a new offering.
entries.note: The source attributes skepticism specifically to potential customers; the normalization turns it into an unattributed general expectation.

entries.test: Contemporaneous investor letters, earnings-call questions, and investment decisions would show whether investors were increasingly dissatisfied with AI spending and returns.
entries.note: Public expressions of dissatisfaction make this broader sentiment claim assessable.

entries.test: Public cloud agreements and hardware procurement records would establish whether OpenAI could obtain the latest compute hardware independently of Microsoft's allocation decisions.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion makes clear that 'technology' refers to compute hardware.
He selects the signal readers should prioritize and defines what he would count as the bubble ending.

entries.test: Public pricing changes, unit-economics disclosures, and investor communications would test whether price increases correspond to investors finding the existing economics unacceptable.
entries.note: The price-increase implication is firm, although the preceding possibility of desperation is hedged.

entries.test: Subsequent funding announcements and financial disclosures would establish their near-term multibillion-dollar financing needs and whether comparable AI firms could raise when they could not.
entries.note: 'No AI company' broadens a discussion centered on generative AI and large language model companies. The record also combines a near-term forecast with a separate conditional claim.

entries.test: Google's and Microsoft's AI investment disclosures, alongside subsequent sector financing and operations, would show whether a slowdown by either ends the boom.
entries.note: The post provides concrete bubble-ending criteria involving major capex cuts or leading-model-company collapse.
Their unprofitability is separately factual, but the financing forecast is qualified by 'likely'.
The prediction depends on desperation and assigns a private narrative-management motive to a future demonstration.
The source concerns moving up Sora's launch, not merely launching it, and hedges the cost comparison and anticipated coverage. The profitability assertion alone is firm and checkable.

entries.test: Public investment and expenditure records would test the approximate $200 billion total, while comparative human-versus-AI evaluations would test the output-quality assertion.
entries.note: An explicitly rough numerical estimate remains checkable; accounting must avoid counting financing and its expenditure twice.

entries.test: Capex announcements and OpenAI's and Anthropic's operating status by August 5, 2024 would establish whether any of the author's defined bubble-ending events had occurred.
entries.note: Read 'as of August 2024' as the publication date, not the entire month.
The record expressly includes his assessment that the two possible outcomes are unlikely.
The source says 'capable of delivering,' rather than requiring actual delivery. Elimination during a tough quarter is only a possibility.
'Could potentially' does not commit to the boom lasting another quarter.

entries.test: Public financing, cloud-support agreements, and operating records would show whether continued survival and continuation of the boom require the stated additional support.
entries.note: This predicts a necessary condition for continued operation, rather than merely describing current finances.

entries.test: Company financial disclosures and public investor demands would show whether generative AI becomes a financial burden and prompts pressure to cut investment.
entries.note: The source says Google, Microsoft, 'or' Amazon; the normalization commits all three. He explicitly expects the antecedent to occur.
The revenue-growth prediction is explicitly qualified by 'likely'; the spending estimate and investor-question prediction are separately testable.
No shared criterion identifies what would make the month 'critical'.

entries.test: Public financial records, training-data provenance and permissions, and adoption and performance studies would test the sustainability, unauthorized-data dependence, utility, and ubiquity assertions.
entries.note: In context, 'stealing' refers to using others' material without authorization; it need not be treated as a precise criminal-law allegation.
The record combines a firm conditional prediction with an explicit possibility of further continuation and an undefined 'crucial' week.

entries.test: OpenAI's financing announcements, investor identities, debt disclosures, and cash requirements through December 31, 2025 would test the amount needed and the asserted necessary funding sources.
entries.note: The survival horizon has passed, and the funding-source claim is categorical.

entries.test: An OpenAI public listing or documented investor liquidity through share sales, buybacks, or acquisition would test the asserted inability to go public and absence of a liquidity path.
entries.note: 'Most assuredly won't' is a firm prediction without a deadline.
'Tough to imagine how' expresses difficulty envisioning survival; the normalization converts that into an explicit likelihood judgment. The possible additional round is expressly hedged.
The shutdown assessment is explicitly probabilistic. The separate assertion about the form a collapse would take is a firm conditional prediction.
'If I had to guess' and 'most likely' expressly hedge the acquirer prediction.

entries.test: Following an absorption, public records of the remaining company's products, staffing, and operations would establish whether it eventually ceases functioning.
entries.note: 'Putter out' has a plain operational reading in this discussion of residual corporate entities.
'Likely' prevents this from being a firm fundraising prediction.
'Only power' adds exclusivity absent from the source. The combined claim concerns private motives and leaves 'another con' undefined.

entries.test: Public product demonstrations and reproducible tests available at publication would establish whether generative AI could provide the described personal assistance or automate spreadsheet and document work.
entries.note: A 'knowledgeable personal assistant' is weaker than the source's 'super smart friend that knows everything about me,' broadening what his denial covers.

entries.test: Subsequent reproducible capability improvements, commercially sustainable deployments, and fulfillment of concrete advertised AI capabilities would test the asserted peak and technological dead end.
entries.note: The claim contains sweeping language but also a firm assertion that further meaningful progress and sustainable operation will not occur.

entries.test: Documented cases of people obtaining practical benefits from large language models would refute the assertion that they help nobody.
entries.note: The surrounding language is rhetorical, but this sentence makes a plain factual assertion.
This is a recommendation about leadership.

'Some form of collapse in big tech' leaves both the affected entities and the qualifying outcome undefined. His earlier definition of the AI bubble ending does not define a collapse of big tech generally.
The magnitude of the error is qualified by 'probably'.

entries.test: Subsequent financing rounds, investor commitments, and the post's defined bubble-ending events would test whether funding disappears and the boom collapses.
entries.note: 'Acceleration' is not clearly technical progress; the normalization selects that meaning without support. 'Seems inevitable' expresses a firm expectation here.
The GPT-5 impact prediction is explicitly hedged by 'likely'; the hardware-availability assertion could be checked separately.

entries.test: Funding announcements and sector investment and operating records for the following quarter would show whether a successful raise sustains the boom for that quarter.
entries.note: Both companies subsequently raised funds, so the next-quarter prediction is due. 'Not forever' does not impose a one-quarter maximum.
The normalization turns 'maybe six months' into a firmer upper bound and supplies a more explicit success condition.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures or credible product-level reporting would establish whether OpenAI's search offering ever becomes profitable.
entries.note: 'I don't think you're gonna' expresses a negative expectation here, rather than an explicit probability.

entries.test: Checking the stated arithmetic would establish whether $195 annual cost per user requires $300 annual revenue to produce a 35 percent profit margin.
entries.note: This is a calculation under stated assumptions, not evidence that actual costs will equal those assumptions.
'Can't imagine anyone' is strengthened into 'nobody will.' The normalization also obscures that his advertising skepticism is conditional on charging users.

entries.test: After a hyperscaler withdrawal, public product availability and deployment records would establish whether smaller-scale generative AI continues operating.
entries.note: The survival prediction explicitly depends on hyperscalers fleeing.
This calls for removal from leadership.
The normalization faithfully extracts the policy recommendation.
The narrative's shifting 'more aggressively and violently' has no shared evidentiary threshold or specified audience.
